summary: The talk introduces AI systems engineering as the next frontier for coding agents, with two takeaways: agents can solve the hardest engineering problems in AI, and this requires standardized repos on the Hugging Face Hub. Ben frames the talk as three escalating "boss" challenges. Boss 1 covers writing and distributing CUDA kernels. Custom kernels were long seen as unattainable for agents due to complex DSLs and hardware integration, but kernel hackathons and papers like KernelBench show agents can write valid, optimized CUDA. Kernel efficiency splits into compute (flops), memory (data movement), and overhead (Python/PyTorch dispatch). Memory is usually the bottleneck—an H100 does a petaflop/second but only 3 TB/s memory bandwidth—so optimized kernels like Flash Attention increase arithmetic intensity to keep GPUs warm. Hugging Face's "kernels" library lets agents distribute kernels as versioned Hub repos with TOML compatibility files. Skills are the core enabler: file-based context that turns zero-shot agent tasks into few-shot workflows. An agent-generated kernel for Qwen 3 8B on H100 achieved 94% speedup. Upskill evaluates skills and compares models on accuracy and token cost. Boss 2 covers end-to-end LLM fine-tuning from a single prompt using HF CLI skills. Boss 3 details a multi-agent auto-research lab inspired by Karpathy's Auto Research project, distributing work across four agent types: researcher (literature scout via HF papers), planner (creates hypotheses and maintains job queue), reviewer (rejects duplicates/stale ideas), workers (implement hypotheses as training script changes via HF jobs), and reporter (monitors jobs, maintains Trackio dashboard). The system is implemented in OpenCode but also works in Codex, Claude, and Gastown. Workers integrate with HF jobs to run on Hub compute with needed hardware, submitting patches back. The reporter uses Trackio, an open-source dashboard with a fully open parquet data layer, enabling agents to access underlying data directly for custom visualizations like Gantt charts. Trackio supports events, warnings, and notifications. Final takeaways emphasize that agents work best with open primitives (Trackio, kernels) rather than opaque APIs, and the Hugging Face Hub is ready for these workloads with storage, tracking, and compute fundamentals in place.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Introduction to AI Systems Engineering
sections.summary: Ben introduces two takeaways: coding agents can tackle the hardest AI engineering problems, and this requires standard repos on the Hub. He frames the talk as three escalating bosses: interactive CUDA kernel writing, zero-shot LLM fine-tuning, and multi-agent auto-research.

sections.title: Boss 1: Writing and Distributing CUDA Kernels
sections.summary: Custom kernels were seen as unattainable for agents due to complex DSLs and hardware integration, but hackathons and papers like KernelBench prove agents can write valid optimized CUDA. Ben defines kernels, notes the installation hell, and asks how to distribute optimized kernels into inference engines.

sections.title: Efficiency in Deep Learning
sections.summary: Kernel efficiency splits into compute (flops), memory (data movement), and overhead (Python/PyTorch dispatch). Memory is usually the bottleneck since H100 does petaflop/second but only 3 TB/s bandwidth. Flash Attention increases arithmetic intensity to keep GPUs warm. Hugging Face's kernels library distributes kernels as versioned Hub repos with TOML compatibility files.

sections.title: Using Skills for Agentic Workflows
sections.summary: Skills are file-based context that turns zero-shot tasks into few-shot workflows. Hugging Face integrates managed skills into projects maintained by project maintainers, with experimental skills in a separate repo. The kernels skill includes benchmarking scripts and references for testing kernel performance.

sections.title: Benchmarking and Evaluating Skills with Upskill
sections.summary: An agent-generated kernel for Qwen 3 8B on H100 achieved 94% speedup, representing low-hanging fruit for hardware-specific optimization. Upskill is an open-source library that generates skill evals and compares models like GPT-OSS, Kimi, and Haiku on accuracy and token cost for skill optimization.

sections.title: Boss 2: End-to-End Fine-tuning of LLMs
sections.summary: Brief coverage of zero-shot fine-tuning: agents can fine-tune models like Qwen 3 from a single prompt using HF CLI skills, fully integrated with Hub compute. A cheaper alternative uses Onslaught with optimized models and free credits.

sections.title: Boss 3: Multi-Agent Auto Research Labs
sections.summary: Inspired by Karpathy's Auto Research project, Ben distributes the research task across four agent types: a researcher (literature scout using HF papers CLI), a planner (maintaining job queue), and workers who implement hypotheses. The section covers the motivation and initial architecture before transitioning to implementation details.

sections.title: Architecture of the Multi-Agent Research System
sections.summary: Ben describes the full architecture: workers implement hypotheses as training script changes, a reporter agent monitors jobs and maintains a dashboard. The system uses a Git project with a main branch for train scripts and a data structure for scores. Implemented in OpenCode but also available in Codex, Claude, and Gastown. Planner creates hypotheses, researchers look up papers, reporter hands information to workers, workers integrate with HF jobs to run on Hub compute and submit patches back.

sections.title: Implementing the Research Agent in OpenCode
sections.summary: Walkthrough of OpenCode implementation with agent configuration named AutoLab. The planner uses a template with current state, job list, successful experiments, and current hyperparameters. The reviewer agent receives jobs, uses a similar template with references and latest scores, gets an overview of failed and successful experiments, and creates tables for inter-agent communication. Ben notes the tables are somewhat verbose and could be trimmed.

sections.title: Monitoring Experiments with Trackio
sections.summary: Trackio is the open-source dashboard for monitoring parallel agent runs. Its main advantage is a fully open parquet data layer, enabling agents to access raw data for custom visualizations like Gantt charts. Trackio supports events, warnings, notifications (including emails for rogue agents), and free-form tables. On the Hub side, jobs run in Hugging Face with labels for sorting and review.

sections.title: Final Takeaways and Conclusion
sections.summary: Two final takeaways: agents work best with open primitives (Trackio, kernels) they can control directly—opaque APIs create a ceiling. The Hugging Face Hub is ready for these workloads with storage, tracking, and compute fundamentals. Ben shares that all examples are documented in blog posts with repos on X and Hugging Face, invites feedback and criticism.
